title: Neuron 489's Language Mixture
takeaway: The neuron whose activations correlate most closely with the Arabic script feature fires on a grab-bag of non-English languages — Japanese, Russian, Spanish, German, French, Portuguese, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Thai — with Arabic present only as a thin red sliver that never grows with activation strength. Where the feature's top activations are near-purely Arabic, this neuron's top activations are not, which is the paper's evidence that dictionary learning did not simply hand back a conveniently clean neuron.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

This is a single neuron of the transformer, not a learned feature. The label `A/neuron/489` reads as: transformer A, the neuron basis, unit number 489 of the MLP's 512 [[neuron-notation]].

The paper picked this particular neuron on purpose. It scanned roughly 40 million dataset examples and kept the neuron whose activations correlate most strongly with the [[arabic-script-feature]] A/1/3450 — the best single-neuron stand-in the model has to offer [[most-correlated-neuron]].

The display is deliberately the same one used earlier for the feature itself, so the two can be laid side by side [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]].

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the neuron's activation level, running from 0 out past 5. Hard zeros are pulled out into their own marker at the far left, because sparsity puts a spike of pure zeros there that would swamp any continuous density.

The vertical axis is density — how many sampled tokens sit at that activation level. Ticks run to 1.4M.

Colour is the Arabic-script score: an estimated log-likelihood ratio $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$, computed independently of the model [[computational-proxy]]. Deep blue at $-5$ means the token is far less likely under Arabic than under the data at large; deep red at $+5$ means the reverse.

So each vertical slice is a stack: at this activation level, how much of the mass is Arabic. The strip underneath restacks the same thing as proportions rather than counts.

The four boxes on top are dataset examples sampled from four activation intervals, tied by dotted lines to roughly 0.4, 2.3, 3.9 and 5.1. Highlighting marks where the neuron fires.

### What it shows

The plot is blue from left to right, and the examples say what that blue is. At 0.4: Japanese, Java source, formulae. At 2.3: Russian, Spanish, German, French. At 3.9: Russian, Portuguese, Ukrainian, Bulgarian. At 5.1: lines naming Thai and Bulgarian.

That is a mixture of non-English languages, not any one of them. The paper reads this as a sensible superposition strategy — languages rarely co-occur, so they are cheap to pack into one direction [[mutually-exclusive-features-in-superposition]].

Arabic is present, as the thin red band along the axis. It stays thin. It does not take over the right-hand end.

That last point is the whole comparison. The feature's own distribution turns near-solid red above activation 5; this neuron's does not [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]].

terms.definition: The chart's title. It plots how often the neuron takes each activation value across a large sample of dataset tokens, with the colour of each slice recording what kind of text those tokens were.
The item being plotted: neuron number 489 in the MLP of transformer A. The paper's running notation writes neurons as A/neurons/N; the chart title uses the singular form for the same unit.
The main one-layer transformer studied in the paper. A second identically-trained transformer, B, differing only in random seed, is kept for universality comparisons.
Here specifically a single unit of the transformer's 512-wide ReLU MLP — an axis of the model's natural coordinate system, as opposed to a direction found by the autoencoder.

The Arabic script feature this neuron is being compared against: transformer A, dictionary learning run 1, learned feature index 3450. It is not drawn on this chart; its own distribution plot is the point of contrast.

The legend title, naming the quantity that sets each slice's colour: an estimated log ratio of how likely a token string is under Arabic script versus under the dataset as a whole. It is a hand-built score, not a model output.

The mapping from that score to colour. Blue means the token scores as unlikely to be Arabic, white means the score is neutral, red means it scores as Arabic. Colour, not height, carries the language information.
The scoring function behind the colours. It uses Bayes' rule plus detection of Arabic Unicode blocks to estimate the ratio, giving an independent yardstick that never consults the transformer.
Count of sampled dataset tokens falling in each activation bin. It measures how often the neuron fires this hard, and says nothing on its own about what the tokens are.
Millions of tokens. The y-axis ticks read 0M through 1.4M.
The neuron's post-ReLU output value on a token. Larger values sit further right and, for a one-layer model, have proportionally larger effect on the output logits.

Two small markers at the far left separating hard zeros from the continuous positive range. The paper splits them out because ReLU sparsity puts a delta spike of exact zeros at the origin that would otherwise dominate the plot.
The short band below the main plot. It restacks the same colour breakdown as proportions at each activation level, so the Arabic share can be read even where total density is small.
Four panels of sampled text, each drawn from one activation interval and connected to it by a dotted line. They let you check by eye what kind of text produces that level of activation.
Marks the tokens on which the neuron is active, with deeper shading for stronger activation. The surrounding unhighlighted tokens are context, four tokens either side of the sampled token.
Connectors tying each example box down to the activation level its examples were sampled from — roughly 0.4, 2.3, 3.9 and 5.1.

Raw byte fragments shown where a Unicode character has been split by the tokenizer into several tokens. Non-Latin scripts are often chopped this way, so a single visible character can span multiple tokens.
Tokens visible in the highest-activation example box. They appear to come from a list naming languages, which is itself a multilingual context rather than text in any single language.
The script of Russian, Ukrainian and Bulgarian, prominent in the middle and upper example boxes here and named in the paper's separate search over neurons' top dataset examples.

The paper's framing for why one neuron carries many languages: the model represents more features than it has neurons by giving each feature a direction rather than an axis, accepting some interference.
A neuron that fires for several unrelated things. This chart is an exhibit of one: neuron 489 responds across a spread of different languages rather than to a single interpretable condition.

The selection rule that produced this neuron: over about 40 million dataset examples, the neuron whose activation trace best correlates with the feature's. The paper prefers it to picking the neuron with the largest dictionary coefficient, since neurons differ in activation scale.

numbers.meaning: The index of the neuron plotted. It has no meaning beyond identity — it is simply the unit that came out top when the paper ranked neurons by activation correlation with the Arabic script feature.
The number of neurons in the transformer's MLP, so neuron 489 is one of 512 candidates. This is also the width the autoencoder is compared against when the paper talks about overcompleteness.
The number of learned features in the A/1 dictionary the compared feature comes from — eight times the neuron count, which is why features need not line up with neurons at all.
The index of the Arabic script feature A/1/3450 within that 4,096-feature dictionary. Again an identity label, not a magnitude.
Dataset examples over which the feature-neuron activation correlation was computed to select neuron 489. A large sample is needed because Arabic script is rare in the data.

Size, in tokens, of the training-set subset used for all activation visualizations in the paper, including this one. Only 10 tokens are kept from each context, so the sample spreads across many documents rather than concentrating in a few.
Tokens sampled per context when building the visualization set — a decorrelation measure so that neighbouring tokens from one document do not dominate a bin.
Tokens of context displayed on each side of the sampled token inside every example box, which is why each highlighted line is a short nine-token window.

Tick marks on the log-likelihood ratio colour scale. Zero means the Arabic hypothesis and the base distribution explain the token equally well; -5 and +5 are the clamped ends, roughly a factor of e^5 (about 150x) against or in favour of Arabic.
The density axis ticks, in millions of sampled tokens. The peak near 1.4M sits at the lowest positive activations, the usual shape for a unit that fires weakly on very many tokens.
Activation-level ticks. The neuron's distribution runs out to roughly 5.5, so its whole positive range is narrower than the feature's, which extends to about 9.

The activation levels the four example boxes are drawn from, spread across the range so the reader can check whether the neuron's meaning sharpens as activation grows. Here it does not — all four boxes show mixed non-English text.
The share of training tokens that are Arabic script. This is the base rate any claim of specificity has to beat, and it is why an Arabic sliver in a general-purpose neuron is unsurprising.
The share of tokens on which the Arabic script feature A/1/3450 is active that score as Arabic. Quoted for the feature, not this neuron, and it is the comparison the figure is set against.

The Arabic share among the feature's barely-active tokens. The paper offers three explanations for the impurity down there: an imperfect proxy, a weak model that is wrong when unconfident, and an autoencoder too narrow to separate every true feature.
The Arabic share among tokens where the feature activates above 5. This near-purity at the top of the range is exactly what neuron 489's plot lacks: its high-activation end stays blue.
The feature activation level above which that 98% purity holds. It also happens to be near the top of this neuron's entire range, which makes the two right-hand ends roughly comparable.

The peak density readings on the feature's plot and on this neuron's plot. The neuron fires on vastly more tokens than the feature does, consistent with a dense, general-purpose unit rather than a sparse specific one.

The number of neurons whose coefficient in the feature's dictionary vector is at least 0.1 in magnitude, reported just before this figure. The feature is spread across many neurons rather than sitting on one.

The count of largest-magnitude coefficients in that dictionary vector that turn out to be negative — the paper flags this with an exclamation mark, since a neuron-aligned feature would be expected to lean positive on its own neuron.

The number of top dataset examples per neuron the paper searched when looking for Arabic-responsive neurons directly. Only one neuron surfaced at all, and only one of its twenty examples was Arabic script; eighteen were English and one Cyrillic.
